item.title: Cyril of Jerusalem and the Lessons in the Dark
item.description: A bedtime story about Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, who taught the people getting ready for baptism every morning in Lent. Tabitha, nine, learns the Creed by heart and not on paper, and asks what will happen on Easter night, but nobody will tell her until afterwards. Then she turns to the west in the dark, turns round to the east, goes down into the water, and in Easter week finds out why they waited. Told from Cyril's lessons and the pilgrim Egeria, with a note for grown-ups. For ages 3 to 8, about ten minutes read aloud. Setting: Jerusalem, in the great church beside the rock of Golgotha and the round church over the tomb, in Lent and Easter, about the year 350. item.title: Polycarp and the Eighty-Six Years
item.description: A bedtime story about Saint Polycarp, the old bishop of Smyrna who as a young man had listened to the apostle John. A boy called Irenaeus remembers where he sat and how he talked. When soldiers come to the farm to arrest him, Polycarp says "The will of God be done", gives them supper and asks for an hour to pray, and before the governor he will not speak against Jesus, whom he has served for eighty-six years. Told from the Martyrdom of Polycarp, with a note for grown-ups on what the letter says, the dove and the date. For ages 3 to 8, about ten minutes read aloud. Setting: Smyrna, a busy harbour city on the coast of Asia (today İzmir, in Turkey), about the year 155. item.title: Cyril and Methodius and the Letters for the Slavs
item.description: A bedtime story for the memorial of Saints Cyril and Methodius on the 14th of February. A prince in Moravia asks for a teacher who can tell his people about Jesus in their own language, but their language has never been written down. Two brothers from Thessalonica, Constantine and Methodius, make it some letters, about forty little shapes for its sounds, and the first words they write are "In the beginning was the Word". Some grown-ups grumble that God can only be prayed to in Hebrew, Greek and Latin; Constantine answers that the rain falls on everyone. Told from the old Slavonic Lives of the two brothers, with a note on why the Cyrillic alphabet is named for Cyril but was not his. For ages 3 to 8, about ten minutes read aloud. item.title: Peter and the Breakfast on the Beach
item.description: A bedtime story about Saint Peter, told from John 21. After a whole night of catching nothing, Peter and six friends hear a man on the shore say "Children, have you any fish?", cast the net on the right side, and haul in 153 big fish without tearing it. Peter jumps into the sea, Jesus has a charcoal fire with fish and bread waiting, and three times he asks "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" and gives Peter his sheep to look after. A note for grown-ups explains the Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, 22 February, and what the old wooden chair in Rome is. For ages 3 to 8, about ten minutes read aloud. Setting: The shore of the Sea of Galilee (the Sea of Tiberias), in the Holy Land, a few weeks after the first Easter, nearly two thousand years ago. item.title: Simeon and Anna and the Baby in the Temple
item.description: A bedtime story for the Feast of the Presentation of the Lord, Candlemas, on the 2nd of February. Mary and Joseph carry the baby Jesus up to the Temple in Jerusalem with the offering of poor families, two little doves. Old Simeon, who has been promised by the Holy Spirit that he will see the Lord's Christ before he dies, takes the baby in his arms and says the prayer the Church still says every night, "Now, Lord, you let your servant go in peace". Then Anna, who prays in the Temple day and night, comes up at that very moment, gives thanks, and tells everyone. Told from Luke 2:22-40 only. For ages 3 to 8, about ten minutes read aloud. Setting: The Temple in Jerusalem, forty days after the first Christmas, about two thousand years ago. item.title: Timothy and the Letters from Paul
item.description: A bedtime story about Saint Timothy, the young man from Lystra who learned the Scriptures on his grandmother Lois's and his mother Eunice's knees and grew up to be Saint Paul's most trusted helper. Told from the Acts of the Apostles and Paul's letters, it follows him as Paul chooses him, sends him alone to the frightened Christians of Thessalonica, waits for his good news, and writes to him "let no one despise your youth" and "bring the cloak I left at Troas". Saint Titus, his friend in Crete, has a small part. His work and death in Ephesus are told as tradition. For ages 3 to 8, about ten minutes read aloud. Timothy and Titus share a feast day, the 26th of January. Setting: Lystra, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus and the roads between them, in the first years of the Church, nearly two thousand years ago. item.title: Basil and Gregory and the Two Roads
item.description: A bedtime story about Saint Basil the Great and Saint Gregory Nazianzen, told from Gregory's own funeral speech for his friend. Two boys from the same far-off hill country meet as students in Athens, share everything "as if one soul had two bodies", and know only two roads in the whole city. Later Basil feeds the hungry in a famine with his own hands and builds a "new city" of care outside Caesarea, and the two friends have a real quarrel about a dusty little town called Sasima, and keep loving each other anyway. For ages 3 to 8, about ten minutes read aloud. Their feast is the 2nd of January. Setting: The university town of Athens and the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia (in today's Türkiye), about sixteen hundred and seventy years ago. item.title: Frances of Rome and the Book Put Down
item.description: A bedtime story about Saint Frances of Rome (1384 to 1440), who wanted to be a nun but was married very young and became the mother of a great, busy Roman household. With her sister-in-law Vannozza she nursed the sick and fed the hungry when hunger and sickness came to Rome, and in 1425 she gathered the women who became the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi. The old story of the prayer she put down four times and found finished in gold is told as a legend, about cheerfully closing the book when somebody needs you. For ages 3 to 8, about eight minutes read aloud. Her feast day is the 9th of March. Setting: Rome, in a big house across the river in Trastevere, from about 1400 to 1440, about six hundred years ago. For ages 3 to 8, about nine minutes read aloud. His feast day is the 25th of August.
